baselineNote: Pre-crisis baseline: how energy normally moves by sea (2025 data, before the 2026 Hormuz closure). Each route carries a sourced volume and its share of that commodity's seaborne trade; line width follows the share. Figures marked ≈ are estimates built from published totals. Routes are illustrative great-circle legs through real ports and chokepoints, not vessel-tracked lanes.

seaborneTotals.note: The denominators for each route's share. Crude and products are derived (marked ≈) because no free full-year 2025 split was found; together with LPG and other liquids they sit inside EIA's 79.8 mb/d of seaborne oil.

crude.basis: Hormuz carried nearly 15 mb/d of crude in 2025, 'nearly 34% of global crude oil trade': 15 ÷ 0.34 ≈ 44 (computed here)

products.basis: seaborne product trade averaged 27.7 mb/d in July 2026, 3.8 mb/d below a year earlier: 27.7 + 3.8 = 31.5 (one month, computed here)
products.source: IEA Oil Market Report (Aug 2026, Kpler data) via Oil & Gas Journal

oil.basis: world maritime oil trade, crude and products
oil.source: EIA, World Oil Transit Chokepoints (updated 3 Mar 2026, Vortexa tanker tracking)

chokepoints.name: Strait of Malacca
chokepoints.flow: 23.2 mb/d of oil (H1 2025), the largest oil chokepoint in the world
chokepoints.why: The short way from the Gulf and Africa into China, Japan and Korea. Narrowest point ~2.7 km wide at the Phillips Channel near Singapore. If it closed, tankers would detour via the Lombok or Sunda straits, adding days and freight cost rather than removing supply.
chokepoints.source: EIA, World Oil Transit Chokepoints (updated Mar 2026)

oil.source: EIA, World Oil Transit Chokepoints (updated 3 Mar 2026, Vortexa tanker tracking)

chokepoints.name: Strait of Hormuz
chokepoints.flow: 20.9 mb/d of oil (H1 2025), ~20% of world oil consumption, plus ~19% of global LNG trade
chokepoints.why: The only sea exit from the Arabian Gulf for Saudi, Iraqi, Kuwaiti, Emirati, Qatari and Iranian exports. Only two pipelines bypass it: Saudi Arabia's East-West line to Yanbu (Red Sea) and the UAE's line to Fujairah. Qatar's LNG has no bypass at all. Most of the oil goes to Asia.
chokepoints.source: EIA, World Oil Transit Chokepoints; IEA Strait of Hormuz factsheet (Feb 2026)

oil.source: EIA, World Oil Transit Chokepoints (updated 3 Mar 2026, Vortexa tanker tracking)

chokepoints.name: Bab-el-Mandeb
chokepoints.flow: 4.2 mb/d of oil (H1 2025), down from ~8.7 mb/d before the 2024 Houthi attacks
chokepoints.why: Southern gate of the Red Sea. Together with Suez it is the short route between the Gulf/Asia and Europe. When it is unsafe, ships go round the Cape of Good Hope instead.

oil.source: EIA, World Oil Transit Chokepoints (updated 3 Mar 2026, Vortexa tanker tracking)

chokepoints.name: Suez Canal + SUMED pipeline
chokepoints.flow: 4.9 mb/d of oil (H1 2025), roughly half its pre-2024 level
chokepoints.why: Connects the Red Sea to the Mediterranean. Fully laden VLCCs are too deep for the canal, so they part-unload into the SUMED pipeline (Ain Sukhna to Sidi Kerir) and reload on the other side.

oil.source: EIA, World Oil Transit Chokepoints (updated 3 Mar 2026, Vortexa tanker tracking)

chokepoints.name: Cape of Good Hope
chokepoints.flow: 9.1 mb/d of oil (H1 2025), up 45% since the Red Sea attacks; the default detour when the Red Sea is unsafe
chokepoints.why: Not a chokepoint in the narrow sense: open ocean, no canal fees, no draught limit. The cost is distance: Asia to North-West Europe takes roughly 10–14 extra days, which ties up ships and pushes freight rates up for everyone.

oil.source: EIA, World Oil Transit Chokepoints (updated 3 Mar 2026, Vortexa tanker tracking)

chokepoints.name: Panama Canal
chokepoints.flow: 2.3 mb/d of oil (H1 2025, fiscal-year basis); key for US Gulf Coast LNG and LPG heading to Asia
chokepoints.why: Cuts one to two weeks off a US Gulf → Asia voyage compared with going round the Cape of Good Hope or South America. Capacity depends on rainfall feeding Gatun Lake: in droughts the authority cuts daily slots and maximum draught, and slots get auctioned at record prices.
chokepoints.source: Panama Canal Authority; S&P Global Commodity Insights

oil.source: EIA, World Oil Transit Chokepoints (updated 3 Mar 2026, Vortexa tanker tracking)

chokepoints.name: Turkish Straits (Bosphorus)
chokepoints.flow: 3.7 mb/d of oil (H1 2025): Russian and Kazakh (CPC) crude out of the Black Sea
chokepoints.why: The only sea exit from the Black Sea, running straight through Istanbul. Tankers queue for daylight, one-way transits, so delays show up quickly in freight and differentials.

oil.source: EIA, World Oil Transit Chokepoints (updated 3 Mar 2026, Vortexa tanker tracking)

chokepoints.name: Danish Straits
chokepoints.flow: 4.9 mb/d of oil (H1 2025): Russia's Baltic crude and product exports (Primorsk, Ust-Luga)
chokepoints.why: Since the 2022 EU embargo, almost all of this flow turns south to India and China, much of it on older 'shadow fleet' tankers with uncertain insurance, a concern for the coastal states.
chokepoints.source: EIA; KSE Institute Russian Oil Tracker

oil.source: EIA, World Oil Transit Chokepoints (updated 3 Mar 2026, Vortexa tanker tracking)

routes.title: Arabian Gulf → China, Japan, Korea

flow.basis: crude and condensate through Hormuz bound for China, South Korea and Japan (37.7% + 12.0% + 10.9% = 60.6% of ≈14.3 mb/d, computed here from EIA's destination shares)
flow.source: EIA World Oil Transit Chokepoints / Hormuz destination data, Q1 2025 (via Statista and Visual Capitalist, 2025); China alone ≈5.4 mb/d

routes.volume: The bulk of Hormuz's ~15 mb/d of crude and condensate; ~84% of Hormuz crude goes to Asia
routes.why: The single biggest oil trade in the world: Saudi, Iraqi, Emirati and Kuwaiti crude on VLCCs (2 million barrels each) to Chinese, Japanese and Korean refiners. About three weeks' sailing. Middle East producers sell mostly on official selling prices (OSPs) set monthly against Dubai/Oman, so Asian refiners watch the Dubai market and the Brent–Dubai spread closely.

routes.title: Arabian Gulf → India (west coast)

flow.basis: crude imported by India through the Strait of Hormuz
flow.source: EIA Hormuz destination data, Q1 2025 (via AFP and Statista, 2025)

routes.volume: India imports ~5 mb/d of crude; before 2022 most came from the Gulf
routes.why: A short haul of about 4–5 days. Jamnagar (Reliance) is the world's largest refining complex. It runs Gulf and Russian crude and exports diesel and jet fuel to Europe, so India sits in the middle of two big flows.

routes.title: Russia (Baltic) → India, via Suez

flow.basis: all Russian crude imported by India (Baltic, Black Sea and Arctic ports), estimated as Russia's 33.3% share of Indian imports × ≈4.8 mb/d of Indian crude imports (Kpler monthly prints of 4.7–5.1 mb/d)
flow.source: Reuters (Jan 2026) on 2025 supplier shares; Kpler monthly data as reported (2025); Russia's total seaborne crude 3.59 mb/d per S&P Global Commodities at Sea (15 Jan 2026)

routes.volume: Russia ships ~3.8–4.1 mb/d of crude by sea; India takes ~38%
routes.why: The flow that the 2022 sanctions created. Urals crude that used to go to Rotterdam now sails about a month to India, at a discount to Brent that pays for the longer voyage. Around half of it moves on 'shadow fleet' tankers outside Western insurance, which is why sanctions enforcement shows up directly in freight rates and discounts.
routes.source: KSE Institute Russian Oil Tracker (May 2026); CREA monthly analysis (2026)

routes.title: Russia (Pacific, ESPO) → China

flow.basis: ESPO Blend loaded at Kozmino (≈4 Mt a month since mid-2025 ≈ 0.96 mb/d; record ≈925 kb/d month per Kpler), ≥85% of it to China
flow.source: Moscow Times (Sep 2025, May 2026); Kommersant / Reuters with Kpler data (2025–26); Energy Intelligence (early 2026)

routes.volume: China takes ~51% of Russia's seaborne crude; ESPO from Kozmino is a big part
routes.why: A 4–5 day hop from Russia's Pacific terminal to the independent 'teapot' refiners in Shandong. Short voyages and no chokepoint make ESPO the most resilient Russian outlet.

routes.title: US Gulf Coast → Europe

flow.basis: US crude exports to Europe: 1.93 mb/d in 2024 less EIA's reported 7% fall in 2025 (computed here); total US crude exports 4.0 mb/d
flow.source: EIA Today in Energy (10 Mar 2026; 2024 edition for the 1.93 mb/d base)

routes.volume: The US exports ~4 mb/d of crude; Europe is the largest destination
routes.why: WTI Midland is now part of the Dated Brent basket, so US crude sets the European benchmark price on many days. Whether US barrels flow east depends on the WTI–Brent spread minus freight: when it narrows, the 'arb' closes and cargoes stay home or go to Asia.
routes.source: EIA; S&P Global Platts (Dated Brent methodology)

routes.title: West Africa → Europe and Asia

flow.basis: Nigeria 1.33 mb/d (485.4 million bbl) + Angola ≈0.98 mb/d (357.1 million bbl), crude exports to all destinations
flow.source: Nigeria: NUPRC 2025 export data via Economic Confidential (Jan 2026); Angola: official 2025 export data via Le360 Afrique (Jan 2026)

routes.volume: Nigeria and Angola together export ~2.5–3 mb/d
routes.why: Light, sweet 'swing' barrels priced off Dated Brent. They go wherever the margin is best that month, Europe or India/China, so WAF differentials are a good real-time read of which region is short of crude.
routes.source: OPEC Annual Statistical Bulletin; S&P Global

routes.title: Brazil → China

flow.basis: Brazilian crude exports to China: 45% of a record 1.98 mb/d
flow.source: MDIC data compiled by StoneX (Agência iNFRA, 8 Jan 2026); Ineep from ANP data

routes.volume: Brazil exports ~1.8–2 mb/d of crude, most of it to China
routes.why: Brazil's pre-salt fields are the fastest-growing non-OPEC supply. Their crude sails about 45 days to China on VLCCs. It never touches a Middle East chokepoint, which is worth a premium when Hormuz is in doubt.

routes.title: US Gulf Coast LNG → Europe

flow.basis: US LNG delivered to Europe (France, Netherlands, UK, Spain, Germany and others)
flow.source: GIIGNL Annual Report 2026 (2025 exporter-by-importer matrix), as mapped leg by leg on the LNG page (data/lng.json)

routes.volume: US exported a record 109 Mt of LNG in 2025, mostly to Europe
routes.why: The flow that replaced Russian pipeline gas after 2022. US LNG is sold free-on-board and priced off Henry Hub, so each cargo goes to whichever of Europe (TTF) or Asia (JKM) pays more after freight and canal costs. When TTF trades near JKM, the cargoes go to Europe because the voyage is shorter.

routes.title: US Gulf Coast LNG → Asia, via Panama

flow.basis: US LNG to Japan, Korea and Taiwan (via Panama or the Cape); a further 6.2 Mt to South Asia goes round the Cape
flow.source: GIIGNL Annual Report 2026 (2025 exporter-by-importer matrix), as mapped leg by leg on the LNG page (data/lng.json)

routes.volume: A smaller share of US LNG; laden Panama transits hit a two-year high in June 2026
routes.why: Only worth doing when the JKM–TTF spread covers the extra freight and the canal fee or delay. Watching that spread tells you which way US cargoes will turn.

routes.title: Qatar LNG → Asia

flow.basis: Qatari LNG to North-East Asia (44.2 Mt) plus India, Pakistan and Bangladesh (22.2 Mt)
flow.source: GIIGNL Annual Report 2026 (2025 exporter-by-importer matrix), as mapped leg by leg on the LNG page (data/lng.json)

routes.volume: Qatar exports ~80 Mt/yr; most goes to China, India, Japan, Korea, Pakistan
routes.why: Mostly long-term contracts, oil-indexed, from the world's lowest-cost LNG. Every Qatari cargo passes Hormuz; there is no pipeline alternative. That is why a Hormuz closure is as much a gas crisis as an oil one.
routes.source: GIIGNL Annual Report 2026; IEA Strait of Hormuz factsheet

routes.title: Qatar LNG → Europe

flow.basis: Qatari LNG to Italy, Belgium, Poland and the UK
flow.source: GIIGNL Annual Report 2026 (2025 exporter-by-importer matrix), as mapped leg by leg on the LNG page (data/lng.json)

routes.volume: A smaller share; mostly to Italy, Belgium, the UK and Poland
routes.why: Normally short via Suez. Since 2024 Qatari carriers have avoided the Red Sea and sail round the Cape, which makes Europe a longer, costlier destination than Asia for them.

routes.title: Australia LNG → Japan, China, Korea

flow.basis: all Australian LNG exports (Western Australia, Queensland, Northern Territory), nearly all to Asia
flow.source: GIIGNL Annual Report 2026 (2025 exporter-by-importer matrix), as mapped leg by leg on the LNG page (data/lng.json)

routes.volume: Australia exports ~80 Mt/yr, almost all to North-East Asia
routes.why: Japan's anchor supplier. The route avoids every Middle East chokepoint, so Australian LNG becomes far more valuable whenever Hormuz is at risk. Western Australia (Gorgon, Wheatstone, North West Shelf) and Queensland (Gladstone, coal-seam gas) are separate systems.
routes.source: GIIGNL; Government of Western Australia LNG profile (2026)

routes.title: Middle East & India diesel/jet → Europe

flow.basis: Middle East diesel/gasoil to Europe (440 kb/d) + Middle East jet fuel to OECD Europe (≈280 kb/d), summed here; India's diesel to Europe (≈160 kb/d with Türkiye in H1 2025, ≈240–280 kb/d in Aug–Sep 2025) is not included
flow.source: IEA Oil Market Report (12 Mar 2026 and 13 May 2026)

routes.volume: Europe is structurally short of diesel and imports ~1 mb/d from east of Suez
routes.why: Before 2022 Europe bought much of its diesel from Russia. Now big export refineries in the Gulf and India fill the gap. This is the flow most exposed to both Hormuz and the Red Sea, which is why European diesel cracks spike first in a Middle East crisis.
routes.source: IEA Oil Market Report; Kpler commentary

routes.title: US Gulf Coast products → Latin America

flow.basis: a floor: US gasoline (Mexico, Guatemala, Colombia, Bahamas, Ecuador ≈639 kb/d), distillate (Mexico, Chile, Brazil ≈445 kb/d) and jet (Mexico, Panama, Brazil ≈79 kb/d) to named Latin American destinations, summed here from EIA shares; excludes LPG, fuel oil and smaller buyers
flow.source: EIA Today in Energy (Mar 2026): US exports of major transportation fuels in 2025 (2.4 mb/d of gasoline, diesel and jet in all)

routes.volume: The US is the world's largest refined-product exporter (~6 mb/d)
routes.why: Gasoline and diesel from US Gulf Coast refineries to Mexico, Brazil, Chile and the Caribbean, on medium-range (MR) product tankers. It's a steady, short-haul business where refining margins and freight decide who wins each cargo.

glossary: Million barrels per day. World oil demand is roughly 100–104 mb/d.
Million tonnes (per year), the usual unit for LNG. 1 Mt of LNG ≈ 1.36 bcm of gas.
Very Large Crude Carrier: about 2 million barrels per cargo, the workhorse on Gulf→Asia.
A narrow passage most of a trade must pass through: if it shuts, the flow stops or detours.
Shipping a cargo from where it is cheap to where it is dear. The arb is 'open' when the price spread is bigger than freight plus costs.
Brent (Atlantic crude), Dubai/Oman (Gulf crude into Asia), WTI (US), Henry Hub (US gas), TTF (European gas), JKM (Asian LNG).
Product price minus crude price: a refinery's gross margin. Diesel cracks jump when diesel supply routes are disrupted.
Older tankers outside Western insurance and ownership, used to move sanctioned Russian (and Iranian) oil.
A contract clause that excuses delivery when events outside the seller's control make it impossible.
